endorsements.title: Key decision points in adopting an AI solution
endorsements.issuer: Health AI Partnership (Duke Health and partners)
endorsements.quote: This decision point features guides for how organizations design and test optimal workflows for clinician-facing AI products.

endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: Important to note, KPNC instituted a mandatory two-week shadowing period before each hospital's go-live, during which alerts were shown to selected clinicians for workflow practice runs (functioning as a simulation environment where staff could rehearse the system before patient safety was at stake).

endorsements.title: Human-centered digital ecosystem: safeguarding healthcare workers' sleep, ergonomics, and occupational health
endorsements.quote: Before comprehensive clinical integration, algorithms must be deployed in a “shadow” or silent monitoring mode to identify hidden systemic errors and prevent patient harm prior to live deployment.

evidence.title: Beyond the Model: Practical Insights from Monitoring Predictive Models across Diverse Clinical Workflows
evidence.outcome: Value of silent alert simulations for pre-implementation threshold selection and performance prediction
evidence.effect: Silent simulations helped select thresholds aligned with clinical capacity and workflows but were limited in predicting post-implementation performance with real-world human-alert interactions.
evidence.quote: Silent alert simulations proved valuable for selecting preimplementation thresholds that aligned with clinical capacity and workflows but were limited in predicting postimplementation performance when the models faced real-world human-alert interactions.

evidence.title: Designing and testing clinical simulations of an early warning system for implementation in acute care settings
evidence.outcome: Whether pre-go-live simulation with nurses identified CDS improvements and training needs
evidence.effect: 6 simulation sessions with 17 nurses yielded four debriefing themes that informed CDS improvements, real-world enhancements, and training requirements before go-live.
evidence.quote: Standardized simulation testing procedures identified and informed the necessary CDS improvements, the enhancements needed for real-world use, and the training requirements to effectively prepare end-users for system go-live.

commentary.bottom_line: Two small studies suggest that pre-go-live simulation may help deployers set alert thresholds, surface workflow problems, and identify training needs. One of them found that silent simulation did not predict how alerts performed once clinicians interacted with them, and no study measured patient harm or alert fatigue after go-live.

perspectives.view: The evidence comprises one descriptive study of 4 predictive models and one qualitative study of 17 nurses. Neither study had a comparison group or measured patient outcomes. The silent-mode study tests a related but different practice, since alerts were not shown to clinicians, which adds indirectness. Certainty is very low.

Six simulation sessions with 17 nurses yielded four debriefing themes that led to CDS changes before go-live, which suggests that rehearsal can catch some design problems before they reach patients. The silent simulation study found limited ability to predict post-implementation performance, so errors that arise from human-alert interaction may still appear only in live care.

Silent simulations helped teams choose thresholds that matched clinical capacity and workflows in a real deployment. Silent mode does not capture how clinicians respond to alerts, and that gap may explain why it predicted post-implementation performance poorly. Simulation sessions with nurses produced workflow and training inputs, which suggests the two approaches answer different questions.

The studies report no data on staff time, cost, or disruption from simulation periods. One framework describes a mandatory two-week shadowing period at each hospital, but no study measured what that period required or whether its length was sufficient. Threshold selection aligned with clinical capacity may help with staffing planning, though the studies did not measure this.

Neither study reported the patient population, payer mix, or setting type. The 17 nurses in the simulation study may not reflect staff in safety-net hospitals, and no study examined whether simulated workflows accounted for patients with limited English proficiency or low literacy.

commentary.research_gap: No study compares go-live with and without a clinician-facing shadowing or simulation period on outcomes such as alert override rates, alert fatigue, clinician errors, or patient harm. Studies are also needed on how long a shadowing period should last, what it costs in staff time, and whether combining silent-mode threshold testing with clinician rehearsal improves prediction of live performance.
commentary.underserved_note: Neither study reported its population or setting, so no test is known to have included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Deployers serving these groups have no direct evidence on whether simulation periods surface workflow problems specific to their patients or staffing conditions.
